question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [New/introduced crop and the Indian region where it was primarily cultivated under British rule]
options: Tea — Assam and Darjeeling (Bengal); large British-owned plantations developed from 1840s onwards
Coffee — Coorg and Chikmagalur (Karnataka); Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu); grown on hill plantations
Indigo — Bengal (Nadia, Jessore) and Bihar (Champaran); forced on peasants by European planters
Rubber — Rajasthan's semi-arid zones; cultivated extensively by the British as an alternative to Ceylon rubber
wrong_fact: Rubber was NOT cultivated extensively in Rajasthan's semi-arid zones. Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) requires a humid tropical climate. British India's rubber plantations were established in Kerala (Travancore, Malabar) and parts of Assam — not in arid Rajasthan.
explanation: Tea in Assam and Darjeeling is well-established history. Coffee estates in Karnataka and the Nilgiris are accurately described. Indigo cultivation in Bengal and Bihar is a key colonial history topic. Rubber cultivation requires tropical rainfall — it was introduced in Kerala and northeast India, never in semi-arid Rajasthan.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [New crop introduction and the colonial policy/mechanism used to expand its cultivation]
options: Cinchona (quinine) — Introduced in Nilgiris and Darjeeling hills by British government to combat malaria among troops
Jute — Expanded in Bengal delta through market incentives; British mills in Dundee (Scotland) were the primary consumers
Groundnut — Introduced in Madras Presidency and expanded under ryotwari incentives for export to Europe
Sugarcane — First introduced into India by the Portuguese in Goa specifically to supply Lisbon's sugar refineries
wrong_fact: Sugarcane was NOT first introduced into India by the Portuguese. Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) has ancient roots in India — it is indigenous to the Indian subcontinent and was cultivated here for millennia before European arrival. India is one of sugarcane's places of origin.
explanation: Cinchona introduction in the Nilgiris and Darjeeling is documented colonial history. Jute's Bengal expansion linked to Dundee mills is factually accurate. Groundnut expansion in Madras for European oil demand is historically supported. Sugarcane, however, is native to India (and New Guinea) — claiming the Portuguese introduced it to India is completely wrong.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Plantation crop, its labour system, and the region where that system operated under British rule]
options: Tea — Assam; indentured labour ('coolies') brought from Jharkhand/Chota Nagpur under Inland Emigration Act 1859
Coffee — Coorg and Mysore; contract labour from coastal Karnataka and Tamil areas; British planters held long leases
Indigo — Bengal and Bihar; European planters used advances (taccavi) to bind peasants to cultivation contracts
Rubber — Malabar (Kerala); plantations used exclusively Chinese indentured labour imported from Malaya under a reciprocal British Empire scheme
wrong_fact: Kerala rubber plantations did NOT use exclusively Chinese indentured labour from Malaya. Labour for Malabar rubber estates came from Tamil Nadu and local communities. No such 'reciprocal British Empire scheme' for Chinese-Malayan labour in Kerala's rubber estates existed.
explanation: Assam tea's indentured labour from Chota Nagpur (under the penal Inland Emigration Act 1859) is well-documented. Coffee in Coorg/Mysore used south Indian contract labour on British-leased hill estates. Indigo planters in Bengal/Bihar used advance-binding (tinkathia/advance system). Rubber in Kerala used Tamil migrant labour — the claim of Chinese Malayan labour in Kerala is historically fabricated.
